title: Book 2 — Euterpe, Chapter 264
paragraphs: Now I think that Melampus the son of Amytheon was not without knowledge of these rites of sacrifice, but was acquainted with them. For Melampus is the one who first set forth to the Hellenes the name of Dionysus and the manner of sacrifice and the procession of the phallos. Strictly speaking, when he made it known he did not take in the whole of it; but those wise men who came after him made it known more at large. Melampus, then, is the one who taught about the phallos that is carried in procession for Dionysus; and from him the Hellenes learnt to do what they do. I say, then, that Melampus, being a man of ability, devised for himself an art of divination, and having learnt from Egypt he taught the Hellenes many things, and among them those that concern Dionysus, making changes in some few points of them. For I shall not say that what is done in the worship of the god in Egypt came accidentally to be the same as what is done among the Hellenes, for then these rites would have been in character with the Hellenic worship and not lately brought in; nor indeed shall I say that the Egyptians took either this or any other customary observance from the Hellenes. But I think it most probable that Melampus learnt the matters concerning Dionysus from Cadmus the Tyrian and from those who came with him from Phoenicia to the land we now call Boeotia.
